documents.abstract: Introduction: This research aimed to evaluate ergonomic risks and musculoskeletal discomfort reported by workers at Agro Fundición, Santo Domingo, during 2026. Materials and Methods: A quantitative, descriptive, non-experimental, cross-sectional study was conducted, covering a census of 13 workers. Data collection involved a 15-question survey, direct observation, and the application of RULA and REBA assessment methods to three critical tasks. Frequencies, percentages, and cross-tabulations of REBA scores were analyzed. Results: Manual load handling was reported as frequent or constant by all 13 participants; prolonged standing, awkward postures, repetitive movements, and trunk rotation were each reported by 12 participants (92.3%). Similarly, 12 participants reported frequent or constant fatigue, as well as discomfort in the lower back, neck, shoulders, or arms. REBA scores were 12 for the casting process, 10 for polishing, and 5 for assembly; RULA scores were 7, 7, and 5, respectively. Discussion: A preventive plan was developed, incorporating engineering controls, work organization, training, and subsequent re-evaluation. Conclusions: The casting and polishing processes require priority attention. The findings characterize the level of exposure and perceived discomfort; the effectiveness of the proposed plan will require future evaluation.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Buildings are major electricity consumers and can interact with distribution network dispatch through flexible power scheduling. These interactions require distribution network operators (DNOs) and building energy managers (BEMs) to reconcile their operational constraints and perform complex cross-field computations. The lack of cross-domain expertise and unified computational workflows could lead to inefficient or physically infeasible interactions. To address this bottleneck, we develop an end-to-end large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent tool, B2G-Agent, that bridges DNOs and BEMs. The tool deploys three collaborative agents: a Translator for bidirectional cross-domain semantic mapping via hybrid retrieval-augmented generation (RAG); an Actor for automated configuration and execution of joint simulation and optimization through directed acyclic graphs; and a Reviewer for memory-augmented reflective failure diagnosis. This workflow abstracts away cross-field modeling complexities and enables both sides to focus on high-level operational decisions. Comprehensive evaluations across 200 synthesized tasks show that B2G-Agent improves the interaction quality score from 66.71 to 85.57 and increases the task success rate from 38.0% to 69.0% over the baseline while satisfying operational constraints. The open-source tool and interface are available at https://github.com/hkuedl/B2G-Agent.

Backdoor attacks pose a persistent security threat to machine learning systems, yet their behavior under graph continual learning (GCL) remains underexplored. Conventional graph backdoor attacks often lose effectiveness as models are updated across successive tasks, creating the impression that continual updates naturally weaken malicious associations. This work reveals a contrasting vulnerability: knowledge-preservation mechanisms in GCL can also preserve early injected backdoors when the poisoned update is compatible with the clean-task signal being retained. For graph data, this risk is amplified by structural triggers, which are embedded into the message-passing paths of graph neural networks (GNNs) and can induce stable representation shifts across tasks. To expose this risk, we propose BadGCL, a model-agnostic framework for persistent backdoor attacks under a strict early-stage intervention setting. BadGCL learns topology-aware structural triggers using a gradient mutual-information objective that couples poisoned gradients with clean-task optimization signals, together with a propagation consistency objective that stabilizes trigger-induced effects through graph message passing. We provide theoretical analysis showing that gradient compatibility and propagation stability jointly support long-term backdoor persistence under benign continual updates. Extensive experiments across task-IL and class-IL protocols, four GCL benchmarks, and diverse victim systems show that BadGCL achieves persistent attack effectiveness with limited clean-utility degradation, substantially outperforming graph and continual-learning backdoor baselines and remaining robust against representative defenses.

AI agents are increasingly deployed in socially consequential settings, yet existing evaluations provide limited assurance that they behave consistently with their intended characteristics across diverse interactions. We introduce an evaluation framework for measuring the behavioral consistency of socially deployed AI agents. The framework operationalizes agent behavior along five measurable axes and uses a standardized evaluation battery spanning six socially salient interaction settings to assess behavioral differentiation, consistency, and drift. Controlled persona configurations serve as experimental anchors, enabling systematic testing of whether intended behavioral differences persist across contexts rather than appearing only as stylistic variation. Preliminary analyses demonstrate measurable differentiation across configurations and suggest associations between behavioral profiles and interaction outcomes. By shifting the focus from persona design to behavioral assurance, this work provides a foundation for evaluating whether socially deployed AI agents behave as intended, consistently and measurably, across the situations in which users encounter them.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Accurate crop yield forecasting is essential for food security, agricultural policy, and commodity markets. Although statistical, process-based, and machine learning approaches have all been proposed, their relative strengths remain poorly understood due to the lack of large-scale, standardized comparisons. We address this gap through a comprehensive benchmark of five modeling paradigms -- statistical baselines, process-based models, conventional feature-engineered machine learning, deep sequence models, and tabular foundation models -- using the CY-Bench benchmark spanning 63 country-crop datasets (>12,000 administrative regions) across six continents. Beyond conventional pooled accuracy metrics, we introduce a multi-dimensional evaluation framework that separately quantifies overall, spatial, temporal, and anomaly prediction skill. Across multiple crops and countries, feature-engineered machine learning and tabular foundation models achieve the strongest overall predictive performance. Data-driven models reduce NRMSE in 72% of countries growing maize and 78% of countries growing wheat, with median reductions of 8.8% and 11.9%, respectively. Across all modeling paradigms, spatial prediction is substantially easier than temporal and anomaly prediction. While data-driven models markedly improve temporal and anomaly prediction over statistical baselines, accurately forecasting year-to-year yield variability remains challenging. These findings suggest that future progress in large-scale crop yield forecasting will depend on the improved characterization of the environmental and management factors driving inter-annual yield variability, founded on effective representations for crop yield forecasting systems that support agricultural decision-making, early-warning applications, and food security planning

RGB and thermal infrared (TIR) sensors provide complementary observations, yet their distinct sensing characteristics make effective cross-modal coordination challenging. Although existing multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can process paired RGB-T inputs, they often fail to translate cross-modal relations into effective task-specific decisions, leaving the potential of these relations to improve task performance and robustness largely untapped. Motivated by this observation, we introduce RelMLLM, an RGB-T MLLM that explicitly learns to exploit cross-modal relations in task-specific decision making. It represents modality reliability, the cross-modal relation, and the dominant modality as a verifiable decision state. We derive task-grounded supervision for this state by comparing RGB-only, TIR-only, and paired RGB-T task outcomes. A hierarchical relation-guided reward supervises modality-specific evidence, relation-state prediction, and the final task output, while encouraging consistency across evidence, relation, and decision. We evaluate RelMLLM on natural RGB-T grounding, RGB-T visual question answering, and held-out sensor degradation. RelMLLM improves grounding accuracy and degradation robustness over its Qwen3-VL baselines while preserving performance on general RGB-T reasoning benchmarks. These results demonstrate that effectively exploiting cross-modal relations leads to more accurate and robust RGB-T decisions. Code and model weights are publicly available.

Context: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) assistants are now part of everyday software engineering work, where developers and students must decide how far to rely on fluent outputs of opaque provenance. Evaluation usually treats reliability as a binary label (true/false, hallucinated/not), which ignores the communicative mode, evidentiary standard, and stakes under which people calibrate trust. Objective: We model statement reliability as a context-conditioned distribution of community endorsement and test whether and to what extent access to verification resources produces measurable, item-dependent signatures in that distribution. Method: The framework represents a statement’s status as a contextual agreement state : the distribution of commitments that a declared community assigns under an explicitly declared context (mode, evidentiary standard, scope, stakes, domain). A bet-based operational semantics makes correspondence truth a limiting case of the framework. In a between-subjects classroom study (about 120 students, session-level random allocation), participants rated six statements without or with external help (web search, GenAI assistants, and other resources). Results: For three of the four statements classified a priori as stable-referent, help raised belief (Cliff’s 𝛿 = 0 . 3 8 –0.43), and dispersion tended to fall (standard-deviation ratios 0.82–0.87; significant for one statement). For both a priori contested statements, belief location barely changed ( 𝛿 = − 0 . 1 1 and 0.07), while responses polarised (ratios 1.35 and 1.48; both significant). The direction of dispersion change matched the a priori family for five of six statements, as did the direction of the mean shift; the exception for dispersion, a historical statement, behaved like a contested one and was reclassified post hoc. Conclusion: Dispersion under verification is a measurable, decision-relevant complement to truth labels and confidence scores. The evidence is preliminary: six items, one cohort, and a composite help condition that does not isolate the contribution of GenAI.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The diffusion of Industry 4.0 technologies, including artificial intelligence, the Internet of Things, and robotics, is transforming manufacturing by increasing efficiency, customization, and flexibility. At the same time, adoption has exposed a substantial skills gap, particularly in advanced technical capabilities and higher-order problem-solving. This study examines the sources of this gap by focusing on misalignment between educational and industry needs, organizational resistance to upskilling, and the rising demand for cross-disciplinary expertise. The study draws on 43 semi-structured interviews with industry and academic experts across 27 countries, analyzed with the Gioia methodology. The findings identify recurring barriers, including outdated training provision, underinvestment in reskilling, and weak collaboration between academia and industry. The results also point to the need to institutionalize continuous learning and to strengthen industry-led workforce transformation through coordinated partnerships and policy incentives. Building on these findings, the paper proposes the Smart Manufacturing Skills Framework (SMSF). The framework links three layers of competence to a continuous learning loop and represents the conditions under which competence is formed, absorbed, and renewed. The mechanisms connecting these conditions are stated as four propositions for future research. The paper concludes with practical recommendations centered on targeted training pathways, government support mechanisms, and lifelong learning strategies to improve workforce readiness for smart manufacturing.

Simultaneous Mandarin speech-to-American Sign Language (ASL) gloss translation requires deciding when an evolving utterance supports committing each gloss. Fixed Wait-k cannot adapt to source-gloss reordering, while training only on reference histories causes exposure bias. We present CausalGloss, an English-prefix-to-ASL-gloss action policy for a Mandarin-speech cascade. It combines lexical and semantic evidence, bounded delay, negation constraints, burst WRITE actions, and incomplete-history recovery. On a frozen 500-example How2Sign-derived benchmark with weak LLM-generated references, CausalGloss improves the fixed Wait-k frontier and nearly matches a three-seed TransLLaMA-style learned adaptive baseline at k = 5 in Token F1 (0.7047 versus 0.7067), with 54.4% lower LAAL. Against CLERC Epee human-gloss references, it achieves 0.649 Token F1 and Pareto-dominates three-seed TransLLaMA-style k = 5 and fixed k = 5, 7, reducing LAAL by 58.2-69.9%. Ablations separate timing from retention. A synthetic Mandarin-speech cascade preserves a smaller computation-aware latency gain, although outputs remain over-long. We also construct ChineseSpeech-ASLGloss-v1, a 19,924-utterance, 36.54-h controlled evaluation corpus.

Attitudes toward STEM develop from the interaction of conceptual knowledge, educational experiences, and affect. Here we use cognitive network science to reconstruct group mindsets as behavioural forma mentis networks (BFMNs). In this case, nodes are cue words and free associations, edges are empirical associative links, and each concept is annotated with perceived valence. We analyse BFMNs from $$N=981$$ observations spanning high school students, university students, and early-career STEM experts, alongside LLM (GPT-OSS) “digital twins” (group-level synthetic counterparts, not individual-level copies), prompted to emulate comparable profiles. Focusing also on semantic neighbourhoods (“frames”) around key target concepts (e.g., STEM subjects or educational actors/places), we quantify frames in terms of valence auras, emotional profiles, network overlap (Jaccard similarity), and concreteness relative to null baselines. Across student groups, science and research are consistently framed positively, while their core quantitative subjects (mathematics and statistics) exhibit more negative and anxiety-related auras, amplified in higher math-anxiety subgroups, evidencing a STEM-science cognitive and emotional dissonance. High-anxiety frames are also less concrete than chance, suggesting more abstract and decontextualised representations of threatening quantitative domains. Human networks show greater overlap between mathematics and anxiety than GPT-OSS. The results highlight how BFMNs capture cognitive-affective signatures of mindsets towards the target domains and indicate that these synthetic counterparts approximate cultural attitudes but miss key context-sensitive, experience-based components of human educational anxiety.

The digitalization of internal control is widely presented as a lever of performance, yet the mechanisms behind this contribution remain unclear. This article argues that the dominant readings of the phenomenon, whether technical, compliance-based, or resource-based, share a common assumption: they treat digitalization as a state rather than as an ability, which prevents them from explaining why comparable tools produce different outcomes and why well-performing control systems become obsolete. Drawing on an integrative literature review and a theory adaptation approach, the article reinterprets internal control digitalization through dynamic capabilities theory. It distinguishes technological resources, operational capabilities, and dynamic capabilities, and defines internal control digitalization as a capability combining continuous risk sensing, deliberate response, and ongoing reconfiguration of the control system. This reinterpretation uncovers a tension between reconfiguration and the stability on which control reliability rests, and introduces the concept of reconfiguration governance, which is distinguished from IT change management and structured around five dimensions. Six propositions follow. The capability affects organizational performance mainly through two parallel and partial mediators, risk management effectiveness and internal control reliability, provided that data are of adequate quality and that automated controls remain under human oversight. Reconfiguration governance determines whether the capability strengthens or weakens control reliability, environmental dynamism moderates the relationship in an inverted U-shaped manner, and institutional pressures weaken it only when they lead to symbolic adoption. The article confronts these propositions with competing arguments, situates them in the Moroccan textile sector, and proposes an operationalization with a view to their empirical validation.

Business process redesign (BPR) has a long-standing catalog of best-practice redesign heuristics, yet, applying them remains a mostly manual task that requires extensive domain knowledge. Despite recent advances using Large Language Models (LLMs) for conversational process model redesign, limitations remain. For example, redesign is user-driven instead of data-driven and is not guided by best practices such as the redesign heuristics. Moreover, only one change can be handled at a time. To address these limitations, given an event log and a BPMN model, we present the DH-BPR framework to realize data-driven heuristic-guided BPR using LLMs. To design DH-BPR, we first conducted an analysis of which redesign heuristics can be automatically detected and applied given information contained in an event log such as the fraction of cases that bypass an activity. Based on this, DH-BPR detects and validates heuristic candidates through a combination of rule-based techniques and an LLM. After that, DH-BPR jointly designs and records an application plan for valid candidates, before finally yielding a redesigned BPMN model and an updated resource model (the way resources execute the process). Evaluation based on simulation using a synthetic benchmark and two real-world event logs shows that the framework's redesign reduces the mean case completion time by up to 61.5%.

Users cannot reliably translate their creative intents into AI-generated music. We contend that the root of this difficulty lies in associative divergence: associations between narratives and musical features are overly remote, and users lack a visible mediation structure to negotiate them. To address this, we introduce five core schema groups as cognitive mediation and propose a bidirectional schema-based framework. Its forward pathway decomposes narrative-to-music associations into staged mappings, while its reverse pathway provides structured interpretations from music back to narrative. Findings from two user studies(N = 188; N = 60) show that the framework led to clearer creative expression and greater perceived control, improved the comprehensibility of generated music, especially for unconventional pieces. Furthermore, it supported cultural and affective thinking while helping users locate associative divergence. Our work points toward better creative intent alignment in human-AI music co-creation.

Algorithmic and AI systems employed in public administration often manifest technocratic and efficiency premises which may conflict with the democratic and socio-technical fundaments of algorithmic practices in government. Partially, these premises are infused into these public algorithmic systems during the design process. This paper conducts a case study in a consortium of Dutch public organisations that reshapes design practices of algorithmic systems to uncover institutional logics underlying these practices. Our observations and interviews at the consortium of 13 public organisations revealed four design practices that deviate from sociotechnical design practices: (1) distance from politics, (2) underrate the input from non-technical experts, (3) operate on a procurement-oriented dynamic, and (4) follow a chronological phasing combined with agile or scrum practices. Through abductive reasoning, we derived the technocratic and businesslike logics that shaped these design practices. These institutional logics clash with the socio-technical, political, and material nature of public algorithmic systems. To arrive at more responsible, accountable and ethical use of these systems in government, public organisations need to modify their design practices. Our findings provide initial insights into the institutional logics required to change design practices, while also underscoring the complexity of altering routines and practices that are deeply rooted in organisational structures and cultures.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The rapid expansion of digital transformation and complex network infrastructures has increased the sophistication and scale of cyber threats, challenging the effectiveness of traditional defense mechanisms. Traditional security operations centers (SOCs) often struggle to meet modern cybersecurity requirements because of their reactive structures, siloed toolkits, and over-reliance on manual processes. Many existing artificial intelligence (AI)-driven SOC (AI-SOC) studies emphasize simulation-based evaluations and seldom analyze the impact of human factors on the operational performance of AI systems. To address these shortcomings, this study proposes a hybrid AI-SOC architecture integrating user and entity behavior analytics, supervised machine learning (random forest), isolation forest, and large language model-based decision-support mechanisms within an Information Security Management Systems (ISMS)-aligned human-in-the-loop framework. The proposed architecture was evaluated using operational security data from the 2023 baseline and 2025 AI-SOC evaluation periods within a public university network. The comparison between evaluation periods revealed an increase in the threat detection rate from 61% to 91% (+30 percentage points), a reduction in the false-positive rate from 14% to 5% (−9 percentage points), a 69.05% reduction in mean time to detect (MTTD), and a 70.83% reduction in mean time to respond (MTTR). These findings highlight the importance of integrating algorithmic automation and adaptive AI capabilities with human expertise to improve security operations in complex institutional environments.

With the rapid growth of space activities, near-Earth space is becoming increasingly congested, leading to a higher risk of spacecraft collisions and space debris generation. Recent close-proximity encounters and collision incidents necessitate efficient and cost-effective onboard systems for space object detection (SOD) and collision avoidance. While deep learning (DL) enabled Edge AI using low-cost vision sensors on single or multiple satellites has shown promises for SOD, significant challenges remain, including limited datasets, small SOD, and the lack of comprehensive performance assessments. This paper presents a collaborative Edge AI framework for multiview SOD and systematically benchmarks DL models and fusion strategies. Results show that higher image resolution significantly improves small SOD. For multiple views, image-level fusion reduces the combined communication and inference latency by 30.13% and 32.80% on average compared with feature-level and attention-based fusion across the evaluated inter-satellite link (ISL) bandwidth. For larger view sets, feature-level and attention-based fusion achieve better detection accuracy at the cost of analysis in the sensing-communication pipeline, revealing that multiview collaboration introduces minimal latency overhead under ISL constraints when reception capacity is not exceeded. Our work provides valuable design insights for future collaborative satellite network design, supporting the emerging space situational awareness and space traffic management requirements.

Introduction: This research aimed to assess occupational risks among workers in the operational sector of the taxi cooperative "TRANSPLAYASA" in the Santo Domingo canton during 2026, through hazard identification, risk assessment, and the formulation of preventive measures. Materials and Methods: The study employed a mixed-methods approach with a descriptive and diagnostic scope, using a non-experimental, cross-sectional design. Data collection involved Likert-scale surveys, semi-structured interviews, direct observation forms, checklists, and the NTP 330 risk assessment matrix, applied to a sample of 140 workers. Results: The findings indicate that the primary risks present relate to ergonomic, psychosocial, mechanical, chemical, and safety factors, with exposure levels varying according to the specific job role. Discussion: Administrative roles showed a higher incidence of ergonomic and psychosocial risks, whereas the mechanic/lubrication technician and the vehicle-owning members (drivers) experienced greater exposure to mechanical, chemical, and road safety risks. Conclusions: Based on this study, a procedures manual was developed containing preventive and corrective measures aimed at controlling the identified risks. This initiative strengthens Occupational Health and Safety management, promotes the prevention of workplace accidents and occupational illnesses, and contributes to the continuous improvement of working conditions at the TRANSPLAYASA taxi cooperative.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: This study examines the relationship between digital platform acceptance and entrepreneurial intentions among early-career digital entrepreneurship learners by integrating the Technology Acceptance Model and Theory of Planned Behaviour. Data were collected from participants across Indonesia and China, recruited through entrepreneurship training programmes and digital business communities, who had exposure to various digital entrepreneurship platforms. PLS-SEM analysis reveals that Perceived Behavioural Control emerges as the strongest predictor of Entrepreneurship Intention, closely followed by Digital Entrepreneurship Resilience. Digital Entrepreneurship Resilience partially mediates the relationships between both Perceived Ease of Use and Perceived Usefulness with Entrepreneurship Intention. The structural model explains 62.5% of the variance in entrepreneurship intention. However, the hypothesised moderating effect of Perceived Behavioural Control on the resilience-intention relationship does not reach statistical significance. These findings suggest that entrepreneurial intention development requires more than technology exposure alone, emphasising the critical roles of perceived control and adaptive capacity in digital contexts. Practical implications indicate that digital entrepreneurship training programmes should deliberately cultivate both technological resilience and behavioural control through platform-based experiential learning rather than focusing exclusively on technical skills.

Abstract Background Giving meaningful feedback on assignments in large introductory-level mathematics courses is a challenge. The emergence of “out of the box” Large Language Models (e.g., ChatGPT, Gemini) has created a potential solution to this challenge, where the AI tool can be trained to give constructive feedback on student work. However, it is unclear whether these tools are sufficiently accurate, efficient, and trustworthy. The current study investigates the use of a bespoke AI tool to assist in giving feedback to students in two introductory mathematics courses that enroll over 400 students each and are characterized by high attrition. Results We evaluated the similarities in grades assigned by the AI tool and human graders, as well as student and grader perceptions of the feedback given by both the AI tool and human graders. We found that the tool was fairly accurate, but that perceptions of the utility of its feedback varied by condition. When evaluated as a stand-alone grading agent, the AI tool was significantly undervalued relative to human graders—both student peers and the professor. Conclusion Three themes that characterize our findings: student trust is key, the professor is irreplaceable, and graders and AI tools must be carefully trained to ensure accuracy, transparency, and trust. We conclude with a call to exercise caution in using these tools in grading assistance, particularly with respect to maintaining student trust and transparency in grading.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: As automated driving systems (ADS) become increasingly integrated into real-world transportation, understanding how human drivers perceive and respond to system failures under adversarial conditions is critical for driving safety. Prior research has shown that human drivers overestimate ADS capabilities and lack awareness of ADS vulnerability to adversarial attacks. We conduct a laboratory study (N=32) using a driving simulator, investigating the effectiveness of explanations on enhancing human drivers' situation awareness (SA) of physical adversarial evasion attacks and their takeover performance in SAE Level 3 automated driving. We varied system reliability and attack object within subjects and explanation between subjects. Quantitative results indicated that explanations enhanced drivers' SA, without deteriorating their takeover performance. The reliability manipulation yielded non-significant results in general, probably because of explanatory content presented for the ADS detected-and-handled attacks. Nevertheless, we obtained the impact of attack object on drivers' takeover control regardless of the explanation manipulation. Qualitative results revealed that drivers often noticed abnormalities without recognizing them as attacks, while perceiving explanations as useful aids for understanding scenarios. We discuss implications of our findings and directions of future work.

Fine-tuning Large Language Models (LLMs) on consumer-grade GPUs is highly cost-effective, yet constrained by limited GPU memory and slow PCIe interconnects. Pipeline parallelism combined with CPU offloading mitigates these hardware bottlenecks by reducing communication overhead. However, existing PP schedules suffer from an inherent limitation termed the weight binding issue. Binding uneven model stages (e.g., the LM head is large) to GPUs limits the pipeline’s throughput to that of the GPU with the heaviest load, leading to severe pipeline bubbles. In this paper, we propose RoundPipe , a novel pipeline schedule that breaks the weight binding constraint on consumer GPU servers. RoundPipe treats GPUs as a pool of stateless execution workers and dynamically dispatches computation stages across devices in a round-robin manner, achieving a near-zero-bubble pipeline. To ensure training correctness and system efficiency, RoundPipe integrates a priority-aware transfer scheduling engine, a Layerwise Model Consistency Protocol, and an automated layer partitioning algorithm. Evaluations on an 8 × RTX 4090 server demonstrate that RoundPipe achieves 1.48–2.16 × speedups over state-of-the-art baselines when fine-tuning 1.7B to 32B models. Remarkably, RoundPipe enables LoRA fine-tuning of the Qwen3-235B model with 31K sequence length on a single server. RoundPipe has been open-sourced as a Python library. Project Page: https://thustorage.github.io/RoundPipe/

topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Degenerative Spine Disease (DSD) is a chronic condition characterised by deterioration of spinal tissues. Although DSD is associated with ageing, it has become increasingly common among younger populations. Despite its incidence, the condition's impact on work life remains under investigation in Zambia. The study aimed to explore the experiences of workplace accommodation for individuals living with DSD and to generate evidence to inform workplace accommodation and labour policies to improve support and social inclusion for individuals living with DSD in Zambia. The theoretical framework anchoring this research was a qualitative Interpretative Descriptive design and included 11 participants aged between 23 and 49 years. Participant selection was through purposeful sampling. Data were collected through face-to-face semi-structured interviews and analysed using inductive thematic analysis with NVivo software version 12. Findings: Key findings included narratives on the challenges faced and recommendations to improve work environments. Challenges included a lack of workplace understanding and accommodation; limited awareness and support in their work environment; inadequate labour laws, as participants described poor workplace policies and a disconnect between what labour laws supposedly are and the reality of their everyday workplaces; and stigma and cultural expectations, which also played a role, though more indirectly. Recommendations were: 1) clear policies and reasonable accommodations; 2) ergonomic safety; 3) hybrid work arrangements; 4) workplace awareness and Education on Chronic Health Conditions; and Regular monitoring, audits, and workplace health assessments. Conclusion: The study established the impact of DSD on individuals' work life and presented practical recommendations for employers and labour policies in Zambia. Future Research: Future research should aim to update Zambia's labour policies to reflect current work contexts and include accommodations for employees with chronic conditions.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly make decisions that unfold over time: autonomous vehicles navigating traffic, robots executing manipulation sequences, game-playing agents taking moves toward their goals, and planning systems constructing multistep action sequences. Explaining such sequential behavior is fundamentally harder than explaining a single classification or regression output, yet this challenge has only recently received sustained research attention across the reinforcement learning, AI planning, robotics, and game-AI communities. This chapter provides an introduction to Explainable AI for Sequential Decision-Making (X-SDM). A unified taxonomy is developed that answers four core questions: what must be explained, who needs the explanation, how are explanations generated algorithmically, and how should they be evaluated. The taxonomy spans formal models including Markov Decision Processes and symbolic planning and covers the major families of explanation methods that have emerged across communities: contrastive and counterfactual explanations, feature importance and attribution methods, plan and goal explanations, model-reconciliation explanations, and intrinsically interpretable policies. These categories are illustrated with representative techniques, and a principled framework for user requirements grounded in situation-awareness theory is sketched. The chapter closes with ten open research questions that chart a roadmap for the field. The chapter integrates perspectives from reinforcement learning, AI planning, robotics, game AI, and cognitive science, offering students and researchers a structured entry point into this growing area.

Generative AI tools such as ChatGPT and Gemini have become part of daily academic life, but little is known about how pre-service teachers use them to deal with academic problems or how teachers perceive their influence on students’ problem-solving. This qualitative, phenomenologically oriented study investigated (a) how final-semester B.Ed. students apply generative AI tools to their academic problems, and (b) how university teachers perceive the influence of AI tools on students’ problem-solving skills and what guidance they offer for productive AI use. Semi-structured interviews was conducted with twenty-three students and thirteen teachers from five public universities in Lahore, Pakistan, and the data was analyzed using thematic analysis. Two student themes were developed: patterns and purposes of AI use in academic work, and deciding between AI and independent effort. Two teacher themes were developed: teachers’ observations of AI use and its perceived influence on problem-solving, and teachers’ guidance, difficulties, and advice for productive AI use. Students reported regular use of AI for assignments, presentations, research, and lesson planning; thirteen tried problems independently first, while nine turned to AI first. All thirteen teachers observed regular and growing use of AI and agreed that it helps students understand concepts and explore approaches, but all thirteen also feared that heavy dependence could weaken critical thinking and independence. Teachers advised students to attempt tasks first, verify AI output, and write final work in their own words. Because the findings rest on participants’ reported views, they describe perceptions and not measured effects on problem-solving ability.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Expressing dynamic events in Mixed Reality (MR) requires users to communicate continuous spatiotemporal information, including entity trajectories, interactions, and temporal dynamics. This task is fundamentally constrained by the linearization bottleneck: human mental models preserve rich relational structures holistically, yet conventional output channels, such as speech, force them to be serialized into sequential streams. Multimodal interaction offers a promising solution by distributing information across complementary channels, but it remains unclear how different multimodal strategies perform as spatiotemporal complexity increases. This paper addresses these two knowledge gaps: the lack of a systematic analysis of decomposing dynamic events and the absence of empirical evidence comparing multimodal expression strategies under controlled-complexity conditions. We propose a structured analysis that decomposes dynamic events into fundamental information blocks and establishes a complexity taxonomy. Building on this analysis, we design sequential and parallel multimodal expression strategies and evaluate them alongside sequential (unimodal) speech as complete interaction strategies in a controlled user study using abstract geometric micro-worlds. Under error-free speech–gaze fusion provided through a Wizard-of-Oz setup, parallel multimodal input maintains a substantial completion-time advantage across the tested event levels. However, its subjective benefits decrease as coordination demands rise. When events include asynchronous timing or causal interactions, parallel input is no longer rated significantly higher than sequential multimodal input, though this does not imply equivalence. These findings suggest a boundary condition for the subjective benefits of the parallel strategy, providing design implications for adaptive multimodal MR systems.

As instrumentation and control (I&C) systems in nuclear power plants (NPPs) are digitalized, cybersecurity concerns have grown. A particular concern is false data injection (FDI) attacks, which can induce malfunctions of plant systems and degrade the situational awareness of main control room operators. Against such attacks, monitoring the integrity of process data can serve as a defensive barrier, and autoencoders have been studied as a promising tool for this purpose. However, their reconstruction error varies across operating conditions even for normal data, which forces the detection threshold above the errors of rare but normal conditions and allows well-crafted manipulations to evade detection. To improve sensitivity where false alarms must be minimized, this study proposes latent-conditioned Mahalanobis scoring, which requires no modification of the conventional autoencoder. The method clusters the latent vectors of calibration data, estimates the mean and covariance of reconstruction residuals per cluster, and scores a query input by the Mahalanobis distance under its nearest clusters' statistics. Experiments with emergency operation data from an NPP simulator and 10 synthetic FDI scenarios injected during accident conditions show that the proposed score outperforms the conventional reconstruction-error score and other scoring methods at high specificity levels.

Despite algorithm-level innovations for multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), the underlying infrastructure for large-scale MARL remains underexplored. Existing training frameworks primarily optimize for single-agent scenarios and fail to capture the graph-structured nature of MARL. This fundamental mismatch leads to three MARL-specific challenges: topology-induced rollout skew, critical path synchronization barriers, and dynamic training demand. To bridge this gap, we propose FlexMARL, a graph-driven rollout-training co-designed framework for large-scale LLM-based MARL. FlexMARL introduces the multi-agent execution graph (MEG) and materializes the intermediate representation as the MEG Store, which provides decentralized multi-table storage and serves as the data hub for system components. Built around the MEG Store, the Rollout Engine develops dependency parallel sampling with hierarchical load balancing, which reduces inference latency and balances intra-agent/inter-agent loads. The Joint Orchestrator exploits an agent-level asynchronous pipeline to mitigate the critical path synchronization barriers while maintaining consistency. The Training Engine achieves on-demand resource allocation by collectively managing training processes for individual agents. The training states of different agents are swapped via location-agnostic communication APIs. Empirical results on a production cluster demonstrate that FlexMARL achieves up to 7.3 × speedup and improves hardware utilization by up to 5.6 × compared to existing frameworks.

Mainstream artificial intelligence systems, particularly Large Language Models (LLMs), are fundamentally constructed upon the Optimization-Driven (OD) paradigm. This paradigm can be characterized as an ill-posed optimization problem within a high-dimensional parameter space. When confronted with real-world scenarios characterized by noise and conflicting constraints, the logic of global error minimization inherently induces a strong smoothing effect. Consequently, this yields statistical compromise solutions that flatten local features, making it arduous to overcome the inherent bottleneck of Out-of-Distribution (OOD) generalization. Existing AI models generate outputs purely based on statistical probabilities. They lack the capacity to autonomously discern truth from falsehood or establish causal logic, thereby lacking genuine cognitive intelligence. To address the ontological limitations of the OD paradigm, this paper proposes a novel paradigm termed \textit{Structure-Enabled Intelligence}. This approach abandons the conventional path of relying solely on computing power scaling and data fitting to achieve emergent intelligence. Instead, it embeds mathematical structures and physical mechanisms as underlying priors into the algorithmic architecture, constraining the model's solving process with structured scientific rules. Through this paradigm shift from ``data-driven objective fitting'' to ``mechanism-structure dominance,'' the proposed approach fundamentally mitigates the issue of statistical compromise, enhances the model's extrapolation and generalization capabilities, and simultaneously reshapes human-AI synergy by upholding human subjectivity in scientific cognition.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Watermarking has emerged as an important technique for distinguishing AI-generated text from human-written text. However, most existing work is primarily empirical, relies on ad hoc watermarking designs, and lacks a fundamental understanding of the performance limits. In this paper, we propose a unified theoretical framework for statistical watermarking of large language models (LLMs), casting the problem as an independence test between generated text and common randomness and jointly designing the watermarking embedder and the detector. Our objective is to maximize detection power while controlling the worst-case false positive rate (FPR) and limiting distortion to text quality. A central focus of our framework is the design of the common randomness, which plays a critical role in both watermark embedding and detection. We characterize the fundamental limits of statistical watermarking under both fixed and optimizable common randomness. Our results show that optimizing the common randomness does not improve the fundamental limits: the best achievable performance is the same as that with fixed common randomness. Nevertheless, common randomness design remains highly important because it can substantially simplify detector design. In particular, with optimizable common randomness, a fixed, deterministic, and model-agnostic detector can achieve optimal performance. We further study a practical setting with fixed uniform common randomness and a fixed deterministic detector, and characterize its performance gap relative to the optimizable case, thereby demonstrating the practical value of optimizable common randomness.

Molecular dynamics is an extremely powerful approach for studying protein behavior, but it requires enormous computational resources to obtain an adequate sampling of possible conformations. Recently, thanks to successes in predicting three-dimensional protein structures, there has been an explosion of research exploring the opportunities offered by deep learning to address the problem of protein conformational landscape. In this work, an artificial intelligence system based on a variant of the Transformer architecture is introduced and applied to the problem of determining the ensemble of three-dimensional structures that a protein can access and their statistical weight. After being trained on a dataset of conformations of a particular protein obtained using classical all-atom molecular dynamics, this neural network is able to directly generate physically plausible protein conformations similar to those obtained both through molecular dynamics and experimentally. The ordered sequence of conformations obtained as output of the neural network rapidly converges towards the most populated regions of the protein's conformational landscape, suggesting that the system may have learned not only the protein's three-dimensional organization but also the thermodynamic weights of the various feasible conformations. These features, combined with its simplicity and low computational load, make this Transformer variant an ideal candidate for the development of systems capable of performing generative molecular dynamics.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has become part of university students’ everyday learning, yet research on its consequences has focused mainly on immediate learning outcomes. This study examined whether the way students use generative AI in their studies is connected with how they appraise their professional futures. Drawing on research on cognitive offloading, appraisal theories of stress and emotion, and career construction theory, I tested whether AI dependence—letting AI do the cognitive work of learning tasks and accepting its output with little verification—rather than frequency of use was associated with anxiety about post-graduation destinations, whether perceived AI threat accounted for part of this association, and whether career adaptability buffered the threat–anxiety link. In a cross-sectional survey of 965 Chinese university students, AI dependence was positively associated with post-graduation anxiety when frequency was controlled (β = .36), whereas frequency was not (β = .00). Perceived AI threat accounted for an indirect association amounting to 41% of the total. Career adaptability was associated with lower anxiety, but, contrary to the buffering hypothesis, the threat–anxiety association was stronger among more adaptable students, and adaptability was unrelated to anxiety when perceived threat was high. In exploratory analyses, critical use of AI output was associated with higher adaptability but not with threat or anxiety. Because the data are cross-sectional and self-reported, the findings are associations compatible with the proposed pathway rather than evidence of causation. Implications for AI-integrated teaching and assessment, AI literacy, and career guidance in higher education are discussed.

Abstract We introduce GenOR‐Twin, a neuro‐symbolic framework that bridges the translation gap between unstructured operational logs and rigorous mathematical optimization. Our architecture uniquely positions large language models as semantic translators rather than direct solvers, ensuring that the system retains the feasibility guarantees of exact combinatorial methods. We design a dynamic constraint injection mechanism (the runtime translation of qualitative disruption events into formal mathematical constraints) that allows the system to structurally modify the optimization problem's feasibility region in real time based on qualitative human inputs. The resulting bidirectional coupling—where operational observations update the virtual model state and optimized decisions are reflected back into the knowledge graph—satisfies the synchronization requirement of a proper digital twin. The framework features an adaptive decision policy that automatically selects between low‐complexity schedule repair and full re‐optimization by analyzing the available system slack. Finally, we demonstrate the generalization of this approach across six distinct optimization domains, showing that static models can adapt to real‐world operational uncertainty.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Agentic AI systems increasingly execute actions for users, including transfers, deployments, account changes, and data release. Human approval gates are meant to prevent these actions from running until a reviewer has inspected the proposed action and issued a decision. Because approval can arrive after a delay, frameworks often persist workflow state and resume later. The resume path therefore becomes a security boundary: it must distinguish evidence that a human approved from approval-shaped values stored in mutable state. We define Approval-Provenance Failure as a condition in which a workflow resume path treats mutable approval-relevant state as evidence that a trusted human approval path produced a decision. Our adversary can write approval-relevant workflow state, but cannot use the approval path, change the model, modify tool code, invoke the tool directly, write the business database, mint a valid approval artifact, or access the approval issuer key. We evaluate 18 agent frameworks with human approval, interruption, or pause-resume behavior. Thirteen are exposed, three are resistant, and two are non-applicable. In exposed cases, state-only approval forgery causes gated action execution after a negative control blocks ordinary resume. The failure also forges the evidence of human oversight itself: across 500 paired audit traces, genuine and forged records are statistically indistinguishable, with exact-match rate 1.0 and AUC 0.5 under the tested native audit-field projection, while provenance evidence separates them with AUC 1.0. Finally, we evaluate a provenance-bound approval artifact that authenticates the decision with a MAC or digital signature and is verified at resume time. The full artifact check blocks 13 adversarial variants on five representative targets with microsecond-scale verification cost.

Operators of collaborative cells have no runtime channel to ask the robot to slow down, leave fragile parts to them or serve them first. Language models can interpret such requests, but their failure modes cannot be listed in advance. This paper separates interpretation from authority: a local model renders each request as a candidate in a small typed language; a deterministic gate admits only candidates that are well formed, raised at the speaker’s own terminal, confined to their zones and tightening; and speed-and-separation monitoring runs below the scheduler, beyond any request. The problem is formalised, and a hazard analysis locates the main residual risk in mode confusion. In a simulated two-operator cell with a Doosan M1013, costs bore little relation to how modest a request sounded: routing fragile parts to an operator cost 1.3% of throughput but raised protective stops sevenfold, and a speed cap cost 6.4%, with almost half of it being borne by the colleague. Six local open-weight models responded within 1.2 s on one GPU and rendered 41–81% of requests exactly. No candidate outside the speaker’s authority or the plant’s limits was admitted, and under the recommended speed law, a full-arm oracle found no breach of the protective distance.

In serverless LLM inference, cloud providers commonly locate multiple instances on a single GPU to improve utilization. However, each instance independently maintains its model weights and runtime state, making duplicate GPU memory the primary bottleneck. Memory deduplication is a widely-used technique for eliminating duplicate data in CPU systems, but extending it to GPU memory faces fundamental challenges. Effective GPU memory deduplication must avoid redundant data movement between CPU and GPU while preserving write isolation for shared pages without native copy-on-write (COW) support. This paper presents gKSM, a transparent GPU memory deduplication framework for serverless LLM inference. gKSM addresses these challenges through CPU-GPU collaborative hash management that offloads hash computation to GPU kernels, zero-copy model weight deduplication that eliminates duplication before model weight transfer, and a cross-privilege page fault handler that combines a lightweight kernel hook and CUDA Virtual Memory Management (VMM) remapping in the user space. gKSM also designs a stable page scanning algorithm and a reuse-aware placement policy in cluster scale. Experiments show that gKSM reduces GPU memory usage by 59.8% while maintaining high throughput compared to ServerlessLLM. Under memory constrained workloads, gKSM improves aggregate throughput by 2.15 × and supports five instances concurrently. In cluster level simulation, gKSM achieves a service rate of 99.97%, compared to 78.2% for SLInfer and 26.9% for ServerlessLLM.

Database performance anomalies in modern production environments are not always triggered by a single cause. Instead, they often arise from the concurrent interaction of multiple causes within the same time window, posing substantial challenges to accurate operator-level root-cause analysis. When multiple root causes interact through shared resources, metric anomalies may be amplified, attenuated, or masked. Consequently, salient local anomalies may no longer correspond directly to the actual root causes, making conventional single-path diagnosis and shallow correlation-based methods prone to misdiagnosis. To address this challenge, we propose HyperDBDiag, a method for multi-root-cause identification and operator-level localization of database performance anomalies. HyperDBDiag connects root causes, performance metrics, SQL templates, and execution operators in a knowledge graph, captures joint anomaly patterns across metrics with a metric hypergraph, and uses a constrained LLM to determine the final root-cause set and provide remediation suggestions. When finer-grained localization is possible, HyperDBDiag also identifies the associated anomalous SQL statements and execution operators. We evaluate HyperDBDiag on a database performance anomaly dataset constructed using DB-MAGS. Experimental results show that HyperDBDiag effectively reduces graph complexity while improving root-cause localization accuracy.

In retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agentic LLM serving, prompts are assembled from multiple independent segments into long contexts, making prefill dominate the computation cost. To reduce this cost, position-independent caching (PIC) admits KV reuse for non-contiguous segments across requests, while hybrid-attention models reduce computational complexity using linear attention. However, existing PIC methods break down on hybrid-attention models because their per-token KV-cache reuse primitives do not transfer to per-request recurrent states. In this work, we present Hypic , the first system to accelerate hybrid-attention LLM serving with position-independent caching. For linear-attention layers, we identify the segment-cumulative transition operator as the missing algebraic primitive and cache it for each segment, enabling near-exact and constant-time state composition. For the remaining full-attention layers, we construct a small seam window to propagate hidden states through the linear-attention layers, so that cross-segment attention can be repaired by recomputation. Finally, Hypic introduces segment parallelism, which parallelizes cache-miss prefill across instances, turning long cold requests into an accelerable workload. Evaluated across four hybrid-attention models and five workloads, Hypic reduces time-to-first-token (TTFT) by 3.25 × on average and improves QPS by 1.66 × over Prefix Cache, while preserving task quality with a 1.71-point gap from Full Recompute.

Universities are alarmed by recent evidence that artificial intelligence (AI) can undermine learning, with students prescribed generic chatbots or centrally designed AI tools performing worse. In a pre-registered randomized controlled trial across 7,200 students at 19 universities over three semesters, we tested whether AI designed by frontline instructors can improve learning. We encouraged instructors to design AI solutions they believed would best help their students. Drawing on their unique knowledge of their classes and students, the instructors created a wide array of innovations. We show that these instructor-designed AI innovations improved student learning, measured by AI-proof assessments (proctored, in-person examinations). We found no change in student engagement, measured by course activity records, or satisfaction, measured by course evaluations. Our findings demonstrate that AI can improve student learning when its adoption is frontline-driven, with instructors empowered to design and refine AI solutions for their own classrooms.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: This study was motivated by the presence of anxiety in the process of learning and using German among university students, particularly when facing communication, evaluation, and judgment from others. This study aimed to describe German language anxiety among students of the German Language Education Study Program at Universitas Negeri Malang. A quantitative approach with a descriptive method was employed involving 63 students. Data were collected using a 28-item instrument covering three aspects: communication apprehension, test anxiety, and fear of negative evaluation. The data were analyzed using descriptive statistics through response distribution and score categorization. The results showed that 66.7% of students were categorized as having high anxiety, 25.4% as moderate, and 7.9% as low. Among the three aspects, test anxiety was the most prominent, with 68.3% of students classified in the high category, followed by fear of negative evaluation at 65.1% and communication apprehension at 61.9%. These findings indicate that German language anxiety among the students was generally high, particularly in situations involving the evaluation of German language proficiency. ABSTRAK Penelitian ini dilatarbelakangi oleh adanya kecemasan yang dapat muncul dalam proses pembelajaran dan penggunaan bahasa Jerman pada mahasiswa, terutama ketika menghadapi situasi komunikasi, evaluasi kemampuan, dan penilaian dari orang lain. Kondisi tersebut penting diperhatikan karena penggunaan bahasa Jerman merupakan bagian utama dalam proses pembelajaran mahasiswa Program Studi Pendidikan Bahasa Jerman. Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk mengetahui gambaran kecemasan berbahasa Jerman pada mahasiswa Program Studi Pendidikan Bahasa Jerman Universitas Negeri Malang. Penelitian menggunakan pendekatan kuantitatif dengan metode deskriptif. Responden penelitian berjumlah 63 mahasiswa dan data dikumpulkan menggunakan instrumen kecemasan berbahasa Jerman yang terdiri atas 28 butir pernyataan dengan tiga aspek, yaitu communication apprehension, test anxiety, dan fear of negative evaluation. Data dianalisis menggunakan statistik deskriptif melalui distribusi jawaban dan kategorisasi skor. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa 42 mahasiswa (66,7%) berada pada kategori kecemasan tinggi, 16 mahasiswa (25,4%) berada pada kategori sedang, dan 5 mahasiswa (7,9%) berada pada kategori rendah. Berdasarkan aspek, test anxiety memiliki proporsi kategori tinggi paling besar, yaitu 68,3%, diikuti fear of negative evaluation sebesar 65,1% dan communication apprehension sebesar 61,9%. Dengan demikian, kecemasan berbahasa Jerman pada mahasiswa dalam penelitian ini tergolong tinggi, dengan kecemasan terhadap evaluasi kemampuan bahasa Jerman sebagai aspek yang paling menonjol.

Entrepreneurs increasingly turn to artificial intelligence (AI) when deciding whether to continue a struggling venture, yet persistence theory locates the antecedents of persistence either within the entrepreneur or within human social networks. We theorize AI as a distinct, non-human antecedent of entrepreneurial persistence. Building on the psychological resource approach to persistence, escalation and threshold theories, and the AI Entrepreneurial Agency Framework, we distinguish two pathways. Through a resource pathway, AI supplies psychological resources that raise persistence intensity and loosen its dependence on the entrepreneur's internal resources. Through an epistemic pathway, AI shapes the feedback on which persistence decisions rest and thereby governs persistence calibration, which we define as the responsiveness of persistence to diagnostic disconfirming evidence. Five propositions specify when the pathways combine into AI-amplified escalation, how the Knightian uncertainty of the decision widens a gap between confidence and calibration, and how agentic AI attenuates the decision points at which founders confront adversity. A temporal extension explains how sustained AI scaffolding can render persistence fragile. The framework reconciles optimistic and pessimistic accounts of AI in entrepreneurship and offers testable implications for small business owners, advisors, and AI designers.

Menurunnya keterlibatan karyawan secara global berpotensi melemahkan inisiatif di tempat kerja, sementara bukti tentang kepengikutan dan perilaku proaktif karyawan tersebar pada beragam konstruk, konteks, dan metode. Penelitian ini bertujuan memetakan karakteristik, pola hubungan, mekanisme, dan kesenjangan penelitian tentang kedua topik tersebut pada periode 2016–2026. Penelitian ini menggunakan tinjauan literatur sistematis yang mengikuti pedoman Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020. Data sekunder berupa artikel jurnal empiris dikumpulkan dari basis data Scopus dan SAGE Journals. Kualitas studi dinilai dengan Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool 2018, dan data dianalisis dengan statistik deskriptif serta sintesis naratif. Sebanyak 21 studi empiris memenuhi kriteria inklusi, dengan 12 studi terbit pada periode 2024–2026. Bukti terkonsentrasi di Asia Timur dan Eropa, dengan Tiongkok menyumbang studi terbanyak (7 studi), didominasi desain kuantitatif (18 studi), dan belum mencakup Indonesia. Hanya 10 studi yang menjadikan kepengikutan sebagai konstruk utama, sedangkan studi lainnya memakai istilah pengikut sebagai sebutan bawahan. Hubungan Followership dan perilaku proaktif terpetakan dalam empat jalur, yaitu anteseden kepemimpinan dan konteks, kepengikutan sebagai prediktor, respons pemimpin terhadap perilaku proaktif, dan batas konseptual kepengikutan. Penelitian ini mengusulkan model timbal balik yang menempatkan orientasi peran kepengikutan sebagai mekanisme penghubung. Penelitian selanjutnya perlu mengukur kepengikutan secara eksplisit, memakai desain longitudinal multisumber, dan menguji konteks Indonesia.

Labor relations in agribusiness present challenges concerning legal protection, economic inequalities, and occupational conditions. In the state of Amazonas, the diversity of agricultural, extractive, and riverine activities adds specific nuances to this analysis. This study examines how scientific literature addresses the rights and obligations within agribusiness labor relations, identifies factors associated with labor conflicts, and explores potential preventive measures tailored to the reality of the Amazon region. The objective was to analyze these relations, identify vulnerability factors, and systematize dimensions for conflict prevention. A qualitative, exploratory, and descriptive narrative literature review was conducted, involving a thematic analysis of 12 articles published between 2014 and 2025. The findings highlight issues related to wage inequality, precarious working conditions, occupational risks, power imbalances in negotiations, and the violation of rights. The analysis also underscores the necessity of distinguishing between formal employment, self-employment, and family-based production. As a contribution, five preventive dimensions were systematized: legal and contractual protection; occupational health and safety; corporate responsibility; equity and social protection; and socio-territorial suitability. It is concluded that conflict prevention requires an integrated approach that considers legal obligations, production conditions, and social vulnerabilities. The effectiveness of the proposed dimensions remains subject to empirical evaluation.

A key challenge in the behavioral sciences is the lack of formal models that capture individual differences in social interactions. At the same time, recent advances in artificial intelligence offer new opportunities to simulate and assess interpersonal behavior at scale. In this study, we introduce an agent-based modeling framework that uses large language models (LLMs) to simulate short-term social interactions. Within a dyadic interaction cycle, an LLM-based agent continually adjusts its interpersonal behavior (agency and communion) to its prior behavior, the partner’s behavior, and the combined influence of behavioral defaults (differences in default behavioral tendencies) and interpersonal reactivities (differences in reactions to partner behaviors). We derive a mathematical model that formalizes how interpersonal behavior unfolds across the interaction, evaluate the model in simulations, illustrate how the framework expresses these interpersonal dynamics in natural language, and outline the framework’s flexibility for simulating individual differences in practical applications across the behavioral sciences.
