Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to design, optimize, and operate the infrastructure behind AI training and serving, yet the literature remains fragmented across hardware design, machine learning systems, electronic design automation, and high-performance computing. We present a comprehensive survey of LLM-assisted AI infrastructure across its lifecycle, from accelerator design and kernel engineering to compilation, deployment, operations, data management, and energy optimization. We organize the literature by the primary resource the LLM manages: artifact-centric methods for computational artifacts, operational-centric methods for deployment context and system state, and resource-centric methods for data and energy. These categories span the lifecycle and cover AI-specific concerns such as distributed-training configuration, inference serving, GPU-cluster scheduling, and data loading. Building on this taxonomy, we conduct a cross-study quantitative synthesis of reported results. Because studies adopt heterogeneous benchmarks, baselines, hardware, and metrics, we compare methods only where evaluation conditions permit and align results along common dimensions: functional correctness, execution performance, throughput, resource and energy consumption, operational outcomes, and optimization cost, keeping each result's native metric, baseline, and setting rather than collapsing them into a single score. This comparison reveals where LLM-driven methods yield consistent gains, how reported gains in workload orchestration depend on the evaluation environment, from simulators to real clusters and production, and where evidence is still lacking. Together, the taxonomy, lifecycle perspective, and quantitative evaluation provide an evidence-grounded reference for LLM-driven engineering of AI infrastructure.

Large language models (LLMs) have proven promising for synthesising loop invariants, a long-standing obstacle to automated program verification. Yet, frontier LLMs are typically accessible only through third-party APIs, hampering reproducibility and local deployment. Small language models (SLMs) sidestep these obstacles but require task-specific fine-tuning, for which high-quality training data is needed. We present a failure-driven data curation method for fine-tuning language models to synthesise loop invariants. Inspired by mutation testing, our approach applies semantic mutation operators to ground-truth invariants, producing semantic mutants that induce verification failure. Each mutant is paired with verifier feedback and its ground-truth counterpart, yielding training examples for feedback-guided invariant refinement. Whereas the vast space of mutants is a long-standing burden in mutation testing, it becomes an asset when generating training data, multiplying the examples obtainable from a fixed set of verified programs. We implement our approach for Dafny, augmenting an existing synthetic dataset of verified programs, and introduce a framework that iteratively refines candidate invariants using verifier feedback. On 472 DafnyBench programs, our best-performing fine-tuned Gemma-4-E4B configuration verifies 50.8% of programs zero-shot, compared to 8.1% for the base model, a 6.3$\times$ improvement. Higher-order mutants prove more effective as training data than first-order mutants, and adding mutation-based examples to direct synthesis examples, in which invariants are removed rather than mutated, improves performance under iterative refinement. Our approach also transfers to Qwen3.5-4B, whose zero-shot verification rate rises from 9.3% to 53.6%.

Patient record linkage is essential for integrating healthcare data fragmented across institutions and systems into unified, longitudinal health profiles that support disease surveillance, research, and policy-making. This study evaluates open-weight language models, including large language models (LLMs), for automating the two key steps of patient record linkage, blocking and matching, against conventional probabilistic linkage. Using real-world data from the Missouri Cancer Registry and Research Center, we linked patient records from a consolidated cancer registry and an electronic pathology reporting system. Probabilistic linkage using the Fellegi–Sunter model served as the baseline. For blocking, we fine-tuned a RoBERTa-based embedding model to retrieve similar records and compared it with a hybrid rule-based and probabilistic approach. For matching, we evaluated RoBERTa and open-weight generative LLMs from the Llama, Mistral, Gemma, and DeepSeek families (3 to 70 billion parameters) under fine-tuned and zero-shot settings. Performance on 52,119 test record pairs was assessed against manually reviewed labels using precision, recall, F1 score, and error counts, with bootstrap confidence intervals and McNemar’s exact tests. Embedding-based blocking reduced candidate pairs by 92% with 99.87% recall, whereas hybrid blocking achieved a 95% reduction with 100% recall. All fine-tuned generative LLMs made fewer errors than the probabilistic baseline (6 to 11 versus 17), although these differences were not statistically significant. Their errors largely differed from the baseline’s; referring only their disagreements to human review would require reviewing fewer than 1% of ambiguous pairs. Zero-shot performance varied widely: Gemma-3-27B showed no statistically significant difference from the baseline, whereas two of the smallest models failed. The reasoning model DeepSeek-R1-70B made more errors and was substantially slower than its non-reasoning counterpart. Fine-tuned open-weight LLMs had numerically fewer errors than the probabilistic linkage baseline, but this was not statistically significant, with complementary error patterns; fine-tuning, rather than model size, made their performance consistent. These models can be deployed locally without transmitting protected health information, making them well suited to support classification of ambiguous record pairs, reduce manual review, and improve completeness of patient-level data for cancer surveillance and research. Hybrid blocking remained preferable to embedding-based blocking for structured patient records.

Organisational learning (OL) and work engagement (WE) are related but conceptually distinct constructs. This critical narrative review examines empirical associations between learning-organisation characteristics and engagement, while distinguishing organisational learning capability from employee training and perceived development opportunities. Searches of Scopus, Web of Science, PsycINFO and Google Scholar were undertaken between December 2025 and September 2026; English-language sources were selected by J.M.A.F. and V.G. The synthesis distinguishes direct observational evidence, adjacent research and theoretical mechanisms. Studies from information technology, banking and other sectors generally report positive but dimension-specific associations, and statistical mediation models have linked learning culture, WE and innovative behaviour. More recent findings suggest that employee characteristics may moderate these associations. However, measurement heterogeneity, possible confounding and predominantly cross-sectional designs preclude robust causal or reciprocal inferences. The Job Demands–Resources (JD–R) model proposes an instrumental resource pathway; Social Exchange Theory proposes a complementary perceived-investment and reciprocity pathway. Healthcare is discussed as an applied context, not as the exclusive evidence base: clinical hierarchies, interprofessional coordination, staffing pressures, emotional labour and shift work may change the operation of these pathways. The review identifies priorities for temporally ordered, multilevel and intervention studies, and provides conditional rather than causal practice implications.

Human groups often fail to integrate information distributed across their members, converging on incorrect decisions. We ask whether large language models (LLMs) can help groups reach the correct decision in such settings. In an online, chat-based experiment, 138 three-person groups (N = 414) completed a hidden-profile hiring task that required selecting the best candidate using public information available to all group members and private information available only to individual members. The randomized human-subject experiment included three conditions: no facilitation, an individual-level LLM that messaged each member privately, and a group-level LLM that messaged the whole group. The LLM facilitation consisted of adaptive interventions that summarized the discussion, nudged quiet members, and played devil's advocate. The LLM did not know which candidate was correct. Both LLM conditions significantly increased the rate at which groups reached consensus on the correct candidate, from 32.6% without facilitation to 56.5% with LLM facilitation. LLM-facilitated groups exchanged more consensus messages signaling agreement on the group's choice. Participants in the group-level condition also disclosed significantly more information about the correct candidate, whereas those receiving individual-level facilitation repeated public information less often. Finally, group-level facilitation received more favorable usability ratings than individual-level facilitation. These results show that LLMs can deliver adaptive, theory-informed interventions that improve group decision-making, and that the design of these interventions may shape how people respond to them.

Large language model (LLM) trading agents now trade stocks for their users, and benchmarks rank models by their agents' returns. Yet a single run's return says little about skill. In our study, two runs of the same model that differed only in the random seed ended 5.2 points apart on average, so telling skill from luck takes many backtests across markets, models and seeds. However, live arenas trade each day only once, and backtests either use the few months after a model's training cutoff or run on years the model may remember, often with news joined to prices by calendar date. In this paper, we present rta-bench-1, a backtest over three US markets (a rally, a bear market and a crash). It shows each headline only after its publication minute, plays each period blind and named, and checks every run for look-ahead. It also splits each return into factor exposure and alpha and scores every decision against random choices of the same day and sector. In 91 runs of six models from four vendors, no alpha was significant, market and style exposure accounted for a median 78% of the return, and the decisions did no better than random stocks of the same sector. The agents bought the stocks with the most positive news, yet in ablations they earned as much without their headlines. Still, the agents carried out rules reliably, since a single cash rule in the prompt cut a GPT-based agent's share in stocks by 30.3 points in all six pairs. Builders should therefore supply the edge themselves and report exposures and alpha, and benchmarks should replay news by publication time.

Specialist training beats generalist scale when forecasting financial statements. To our knowledge, no prior work jointly forecasts complete financial statements beyond one year, yet in a discounted-cash-flow valuation most firm value sits past that window. We release ProForma-20Q, a reproducible benchmark for forecasting 78 statement line items 1–20 quarters ahead, for anonymized firms, from past statements and an industry code, scored by change-space R2. On it, Forma, a transformer that reads statements as sets of (account, quarter, value) tuples and maximizes a masked-tuple Gaussian likelihood, beats every competitor we field: classical machine learning, chained gradient boosting, a zero-shot time-series foundation model, and frontier large language models. Its lead widens with horizon, where valuation needs accuracy most, and its Gaussian predictive intervals never under-cover. Forma’s forecasts nearly satisfy accounting identities; exact coherence is recoverable at a small accuracy cost. Its tuple interface supports scenario analysis without retraining, and we show that pinning future revenue paths sharpens the rest of the statement.

LLM-based architectures offer strong generalization and instruction-following capabilities for streaming automatic speech recognition (ASR), but multi-talker use introduces coupled transcription, attribution, and latency challenges. Our wearable setting requires real-time transcription of a conversation between a near-field device wearer and a far-field partner. Because partial hypotheses are rendered on persistent sides of a dialogue UI, speaker roles cannot be permuted and each speaker tag must precede its turn. These sparse tags are weakly optimized by supervised fine-tuning (SFT), while committing to a leading tag can delay the text that follows. We therefore post-train a streaming LLM-based ASR model with reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), combining a fixed-role Speaker-Attributed WER (SA-WER) grader with a turn-level onset-delay reward. On an eight-direction multi-talker cohort, SA-WER RL reduces SA-WER from $20.51\%$ for SFT to $13.14\%$. Adding the delay objective reduces onset $p50$ by $65\%$ (from $0.918\,\text{s}$ to $0.320\,\text{s}$) and $p90$ by $44\%$ (from $1.389\,\text{s}$ to $0.780\,\text{s}$) relative to SA-WER-only RL, while achieving $12.70\%$ SA-WER. These results demonstrate that fixed-role recognition quality and streaming responsiveness can be improved jointly.

Work-related mental disorders have become one of the leading causes of occupational leave among healthcare professionals, particularly in nursing, due to work overload, long working hours, institutional pressure, and constant exposure to situations of suffering. Considering this scenario, this study aimed to analyze the epidemiological profile of leaves of absence due to mental and behavioral disorders among nursing professionals in the state of Santa Catarina, Brazil, from 2020 to 2024. To this end, a quantitative, descriptive, and epidemiological study was conducted using secondary data from the National Observatory of Occupational Health and Safety (SmartLab), regarding absences classified under ICD-10 codes F00–F99, analyzed through descriptive statistics. The findings revealed variations in the number of absences throughout the study period, with an initial reduction followed by a significant increase in the final years of the historical series. Depressive disorders, anxiety disorders, and stress-related and adjustment disorders were the most prevalent diagnoses. Nursing technicians represented the professional category with the highest number of absences, followed by nursing assistants and registered nurses. It is concluded that mental health-related absences show an increasing trend, highlighting the impact of working conditions on the mental health of nursing professionals and reinforcing the need for preventive measures, mental health promotion strategies, and improvements in workplace conditions.

AI-literacy training may facilitate workplace adoption of GenAI, yet little is known about how employees’ motivational beliefs change during training. Drawing on expectancy-value theory, we examined motivation before and after Hazlo con IA, a national adaptive AI-literacy program in Chile. The baseline sample included 9,835 working adults across public, healthcare, and small and medium-sized enterprise sectors (SME); 1,864 provided matched pretest–posttest responses. At both time points, attainment value (B = .231–.234), intrinsic value (B = .156–.173), utility value (B = .113–.185), and perceived workplace support (B = .153–.184) positively predicted intentions to use GenAI (all ps < .001). Self-efficacy was positively associated with intentions only at posttest (B = .086, p = .004), whereas perceived costs and anxiety were not significant independent predictors. Following training, all measured constructs except perceived workplace support declined significantly, although effects were small; the largest standardized decline was in intention to use AI (ΔM = −.193, dz = −.29, p < .001). Age (V = .016, p < .001) and employment sector (V = .020, p = .005) showed small multivariate associations with change: older participants reported slightly greater declines in workplace support (B = −.0054), and public-sector employees showed larger declines in intentions than SME employees (ΔM = −.240 vs. −.061, p = .004). Other demographic and experience variables were not significant. These findings highlight the central role of subjective value in workplace GenAI intentions and the relative stability of motivational beliefs across demographic and occupational contexts.
topics: Human Resource Development and Performance Evaluation
